_comment: The routing VOCABULARY for Toolbay Stack. Toolbay Stack, Copyright (c) 2026 Toolbay. MIT. Original work.
This file does not name a single skill, and that is the whole point. gstack routes
with a hand-written table of the form 'User asks to ship, deploy, push -> invoke /ship'.
That table names skills, so renaming or removing a skill leaves a stale rule behind, and
in gstack 1.60.1.0 it has already drifted: the same file carries two copies of the table,
one with 13 rules and one with 35, and they disagree.
Here the mapping is request-phrase -> CAPABILITY, and skills declare which capabilities
they provide in their own frontmatter. The skill side of the mapping is read off disk at
route time, so a skill that is gone cannot be routed to and a skill that is added needs no
edit here. This file only goes stale if English does.

work-mode.label: set or read the stance the work is being done in
work-mode._why: A stance is not a task, so it needs its own token. 'what mode am I in' and 'be careful with this' are different requests: one reads the stance layer, the other asks for a safety hook.

next-step-suggestion.label: read the project as it is now and say what is worth doing next
next-step-suggestion._why: Distinct from skill-routing, which answers 'which skill handles THIS request'. Here there is no request yet: the input is the repository, and the output is what is worth doing at all, including 'nothing'. It needs its own token because the two questions have opposite shapes, and because the honest answer is often that there is no answer, which no other capability here is allowed to give.
next-step-suggestion._matchNote: "where did i leave off" is deliberately NOT here. It is a request to reload saved state, not a request for something new to do, and while both tokens carried it the two skills sat one point apart. It lives in context-restore-verification only. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

user-memory.label: keep, recall, or delete what this person has told the agent about how they work
user-memory._why: Separate from every other token here because the input is not a task at all, it is the user pushing back on one. 'no, not like that' and 'I already told you' are the two highest-signal sentences a session contains, and they route nowhere in a stack that only maps requests to work. This token also has to cover the opposite direction, 'what do you have on me' and 'forget that', because a memory you cannot interrogate or delete is one people are right to refuse.
match: what do you know about me
what do you have on me

qa-testing.label: test a running application
qa-testing._matchNote: "check the deploy" and "verify the deploy" were here and are not any more. /qa fixes what it finds and /land-and-deploy runs `gh pr merge`, so those two read-only questions were routing a look at production to a skill that writes to it. They belong to deploy-verification, which is owned by /canary. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

qa-report-only.label: audit an application without changing it
qa-report-only._why: A separate token from qa-testing on purpose. 'QA it' and 'QA it but do not touch anything' are different jobs with different blast radii, and folding them together is how a router answers 'audit the client's app, read only' with the skill that commits fixes.

debugging.label: find the root cause of a defect

code-review.label: review a change before it lands

design-system.label: define a design system or visual identity

spec-authoring.label: turn intent into an executable spec

security-control-verification.label: prove a security control was actually checked
security-control-verification._why: Separate from security-audit because 'did that check even run' is a different request from 'audit me'. An audit that could not reach a control must report it as unverified, and asking for that is asking for a specific behaviour, not a general scan.

skill-supply-chain-audit.label: scan installed agent skills for malicious instructions
skill-supply-chain-audit._why: SKILL.md is executable prompt code, not documentation, so 'is this skill safe to install' is its own capability and not a subset of code review.

edit-boundary-guard.label: restrict which files can be edited

edit-boundary-release.label: lift an edit restriction
edit-boundary-release._why: The opposite of edit-boundary-guard, and a separate token because it is a separate operation. Folding both into one capability is how a router answers 'unfreeze' with /freeze.

safety-hook-verification.label: prove a safety hook is really active

context-write.label: write the working context of this session down so a later one can read it
context-write._why: Split out of a single context-checkpoint token, which both /context-save and /context-restore declared. One token for both directions meant the router scored them identically on every phrase and the only thing separating them was one verbatim trigger string, so a request that missed that string was a coin flip between the skill that writes a file and the skill that overwrites the model's beliefs from one. Save and restore are opposite operations with opposite failure modes, so they get opposite tokens.

context-read.label: load a working context that was written down earlier
context-read._why: The read half of the pair that used to share one token with the write half. Kept distinct from context-restore-verification, which asks whether a context already loaded still describes reality: this one is the request to load it at all.

ios-development.label: build, run, or test an iOS app

scraping.label: pull structured data off a web page

marketplace-search.label: find a packaged capability someone already built

skill-routing.label: decide which skill handles a request

visual-evidence-ledger.label: back a visual claim with a screenshot that opens
visual-evidence-ledger._why: Separate from design-review because the request is about proof, not taste. 'Show me' and 'prove the fix worked' should reach the skill that refuses a 0-byte or blank screenshot, not a skill that will describe the page again.

contrast-audit.label: measure colour contrast against WCAG
contrast-audit._why: A ratio is arithmetic on two colours. Routing it here means the answer is computed, not estimated off a screenshot.

page-evidence.label: prove one page actually loaded, with an artifact
page-evidence._why: Distinct from browser-automation (drive a browser through a flow) and from qa-testing (walk a whole app). This is the narrow ask: load one URL and come back with a verdict backed by a file that opens. It needs its own token because the honest answer is computed from output that exists, and a page that never loaded has to fail rather than read clean.

deploy-verification.label: prove the deploy actually landed, not just that a URL answers
deploy-verification._why: Distinct from shipping-deploy (do the deploy) and from page-evidence (prove one page loaded). This is the commit-level question: is the URL serving THIS merge commit. It needs its own token because the failure it catches looks healthy from the outside. A paused Vercel account keeps serving the previous build at 200, fast, with a clean console, so every liveness check passes while production is a build behind. Routing that to a page-load check would answer the wrong question convincingly.
deploy-verification._matchNote: The four merge-shaped phrases that used to live here ("land the pr", "merge and deploy", "revert the merge", "roll back the deploy") moved to merge-landing-proof. They are requests to DO the landing, and leaving them on a verification token had two skills tied on every deploy question. This token is now owned by /canary alone. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

merge-landing-proof.label: merge the change and prove the production URL is serving that exact merge commit
merge-landing-proof._why: The narrow half of shipping that deploy-verification kept swallowing. Distinct from shipping-deploy, which is the whole errand of getting a change out, and from deploy-verification, which observes production without touching it. The defining fact here is that the merge commit is the reference: the question is not 'is the site healthy' but 'is the SHA that this merge produced the SHA being served', and the honest failures are merge-shaped — a merge that never happened, a build that exited 0 without aliasing, a revert that has to go back through the same gate. It needs its own token because the request is an instruction with a write in it, so it must never be reachable from a read-only question about production.

design-exploration.label: generate several design directions and choose between them by eye
design-exploration._why: Distinct from design-system (define the rules once) and design-review (audit one existing screen). This is the fork in the road: several candidates exist and a human picks one. It needs its own token because the deliverable is a comparison, and a comparison built from variants that failed to generate, or that are near-duplicates of each other, is a choice the user never actually got to make.
match: do not like how this looks

plan-review-pipeline.label: run every plan review end to end with the decisions made for you
plan-review-pipeline._why: Distinct from planning-review, which is one reviewer looking at a plan. This is the gauntlet plus the authority to answer its questions: the user is handing over the intermediate decisions, not just asking for an opinion. It needs its own token because the two requests want different skills and 'don't ask me' is the part that decides which.

review-evidence-gate.label: prove a review actually produced the outputs it claims
review-evidence-gate._why: A review that reports itself complete and a review that is complete are different states, and only one of them is checkable. Separate from code-review and planning-review because the request is not 'review this', it is 'was that review real'. The failure it catches reads as success: a summary, a consensus table of placeholder dashes, and a passing log entry, with none of the required artifacts on disk.

context-save-verification.label: prove a saved working context actually landed on disk and can still be read
context-save-verification._why: Separate from context-write (do the save) because the request is about the artifact, not the act. 'Did that save actually work' and 'where is it' are asked precisely when the drawer looks empty, and the failure they catch reads as success: on Windows gstack's save resolves its own MSYS state path to C:\c\Users\..., its list step runs find.exe and reports 'no saved contexts yet' next to files that exist, and the banner prints either way. Routing that here reaches the skill that re-reads the file and checksums it rather than one that will describe the save again.

skill-codification.label: turn a flow that worked once into a permanent, tested artifact on disk
skill-codification._why: Distinct from spec-authoring (write down what to build) and from scraping (do the pull this time). The input here is a thing that ALREADY worked and the output is a durable artifact plus the test that keeps it honest. It needs its own token because the failure it guards against is a skill that lands on disk looking finished, which is worse than no skill: every later run reaches for it instead of re-deriving the answer.
match: i don't want to figure this out again
i do not want to figure this out again
so i never have to do this again

generated-test-quality-gate.label: prove a generated test would actually catch the thing breaking
generated-test-quality-gate._why: Separate from code-review and qa-testing because the subject is the test, not the code. A test that passes on a gutted input is indistinguishable from a good one in every report that only prints exit codes, so 'does that test test anything' is a question that needs a skill which answers it by breaking the input on purpose, not one that reads the assertions and forms an opinion.

uptime-monitoring.label: watch a live url over a window of time, not once
uptime-monitoring._why: Distinct from deploy-verification (is the right build serving) and page-evidence (did this page load). The defining word is DURATION: the answer needs repeated observations across minutes, because the failures it catches are intermittent, warm-up-only, or arrive a few minutes after the deploy when a cache expires. A single check answers a different question and answers it too early.

scope-posture.label: decide how ambitious this plan should be before reviewing it
scope-posture._why: Distinct from planning-review, which answers 'is this plan any good'. This request is upstream of that one: it asks how much to build at all, and the four honest answers (dream bigger, hold and cherry-pick, hold and harden, cut to the bone) lead to four different reviews of the same plan. It needs its own token because the posture is a decision the user owns, and a router that folds it into 'review the plan' hands back an opinion where a fork in the road was asked for.

plan-report-gate.label: prove a plan review wrote its report before the plan is presented
plan-report-gate._why: Separate from review-evidence-gate, which asks whether a whole pipeline produced its per-phase outputs. This is the narrow end-of-review question about one file: is the review report actually in the plan, is it the last section, is its table filled, does the file end with the unresolved-decisions status. It needs its own token because the failure it catches reads as success from inside the conversation - review prose in the plan body feels finished and is not the report.

deploy-target-detection.label: work out from the repository itself what actually deploys it
deploy-target-detection._why: Distinct from shipping-deploy (do the deploy) and deploy-verification (prove the deploy landed). Here nothing is being deployed: the question is what the deploy path even IS, and the answer is read off disk. It needs its own token because the honest answer is often 'two platforms have evidence and I will not pick for you', and every other deploy capability is obliged to come back with one confident answer.

deploy-configuration.label: record how a project deploys, once, so later deploys can be checked against it
deploy-configuration._why: The setup half of shipping, and a separate token because it is the only deploy capability that WRITES a claim about the future rather than reading the present. The failure it prevents is silent and delayed: a trigger recorded as 'deploys automatically on push' in a repository that has no git remote reads fine, survives review, and surfaces weeks later as a merge that never reached production.

idea-diagnostic.label: pressure-test an idea before anything is built
idea-diagnostic._why: Distinct from planning-review, which reads a plan that already exists, and from spec-authoring, which writes a ticket for something already decided. Here there is no plan and no ticket: the input is an intention, and the output may be that the thing is not worth building. It needs its own token because it is the only capability whose success case includes talking the user out of the work.

design-doc-authoring.label: produce the design doc that the later reviews read
design-doc-authoring._why: The artifact, not the conversation. Separate from spec-authoring because a spec commits to one approach and a design doc is where the alternatives, the premises and the rejected paths live, and the plan reviews downstream read the second one. It needs its own token because 'write this up' after a brainstorm and 'file a ticket' want different skills and different templates.
match: write it up as a design
what are the options for building

relationship-continuity.label: know whether we have done this before, and refuse to guess
relationship-continuity._why: Separate from context-read, which resumes the state of the WORK. This is state about the person: how many sessions, what was assigned last time, what has already been recommended. It needs its own token because the failure it catches reads as warmth rather than as an error. A history that cannot be read is not a new user, and treating it as one replays a first-meeting introduction at someone on session forty and re-recommends everything they have already seen.
match: did we talk about this already

extraction-evidence.label: prove the rows actually came off the page they are claimed to come from
extraction-evidence._why: Distinct from scraping (go and get the data) and from page-evidence (prove one page loaded). This is the question asked afterwards: are these rows real. It needs its own token because the failure it catches reads as a clean result. Handed an empty or blocked page and asked for JSON, a model returns {"items":[],"count":0}, which is indistinguishable from a page that genuinely has nothing on it. Routing that to a general scraper answers by scraping again, which produces the same empty answer with more confidence.
match: where did this data come from

structured-data-export.label: turn a page into a file another tool can open
structured-data-export._why: Separate from scraping because the deliverable is the file, not the answer in chat. 'Get me the prices' and 'get me a CSV of the prices' end differently: one is prose, the other has to exist on disk, have one row per record, and open as a table in Excel on Windows rather than as one column of mojibake. A skill that answers in chat has not done the second job.

bot-wall-detection.label: tell a blocked, empty, or still-loading page apart from a page with no results
bot-wall-detection._why: These are opposite answers that look identical downstream: 'there are no listings' and 'you never saw the listings'. A Cloudflare interstitial, a soft 404 serving 200, a JS shell, and a skeleton screen of identical placeholder rows are all valid HTML that parse cleanly and contain no data. It needs its own token because acting on the wrong one of those is how an outreach or competitor-research run quietly builds a dataset of nothing and reports it as a finding.

context-restore-verification.label: reload saved working context only after checking it still describes reality
context-restore-verification._why: Separate from context-read, which is the request to load a saved context at all. This is the direction of that pair where being wrong is invisible: what a restore prints BECOMES what the model believes about the project, so a restore that looked in the wrong directory, or loaded a file that is not a saved context at all, does not fail loudly, it misleads for the rest of the session. The failure it catches reads as success: a full RESUMING banner with a title, a branch, a saved-at time and a remaining-work list, describing files deleted weeks ago on a branch that no longer exists. It also needs its own token because 'is that still accurate' is a question about a context already loaded, not a request to load one.

webfont-verification.label: prove a proposed typeface can actually be loaded before anyone signs off on it
webfont-verification._why: Separate from design-system (choose the faces) because the question is not aesthetic, it is whether the file exists on a server. It needs its own token because the failure it catches is invisible by construction: a stylesheet link for a family its provider does not serve returns HTTP 400, the browser silently renders the next family in the stack, and nothing on the page, in the console, or in the agent's output says so. Measured 2026-08-13, four of the six display faces gstack recommends return 400 from the Google Fonts API gstack tells you to load them from, so 'which provider serves this font' is a question that has to be answered by a request, not by a memory.
match: where does that font come from

performance-regression-gate.label: decide whether a change made it slower or heavier, against stored numbers, with a threshold that can fail the run
performance-regression-gate._why: Distinct from performance-benchmark, which is 'how fast is it right now'. This request is comparative and its answer has to be a gate: a number next to a stored number, judged by a rule, with an exit code something downstream can act on. It needs its own token because the failure it catches is the reassuring kind. A benchmark whose measurement silently returned nothing prints the metrics it does have and reads as clean, a baseline captured after the slow change landed makes the slow numbers the reference point forever, and a build that broke and now serves a 4KB error page in place of a 700KB app scores as an improvement on every threshold that only fires upward.

design-system-preview.label: render a proposed design system as a page you can look at, and prove the page is showing what it claims
design-system-preview._why: Distinct from design-system (decide the rules), design-exploration (pick between directions) and design-review (audit a screen that already exists). The deliverable here is one artifact whose whole purpose is to be believed: a specimen page someone approves typography and colour from. It needs its own token because approving the wrong artifact is silent and expensive — a preview that fell back to a system font, or that was written to a path the opener could not find, looks exactly like a preview that worked.

ios-debug-bridge-sync.label: bring an iOS app's debug instrumentation back in line with the upstream templates it came from
ios-debug-bridge-sync._why: Distinct from ios-development, which is building and testing the app itself. Here the subject is the instrumentation, not the product: files that were copied in from somewhere else and have drifted since. It needs its own token because the request is asked precisely when nobody knows what state those files are in, and the answer that reads best is the one that is wrong. Two absent version files compare equal, so 'already up to date' is what an unchecked install reports.
match: debug overlay is out of date
is the ios bridge up to date

generated-code-drift.label: tell an upstream change apart from a local edit in a file that was generated or copied in
generated-code-drift._why: Separate from code-review, which reads a diff someone wrote on purpose. A generated or vendored file has two authors, and the only question that matters is which of them moved. Folding the two into one answer is how a resync silently reverts a fix someone made by hand, or overwrites a rendered file with the raw template it was rendered from and stops the build. The honest verdict here is often 'both changed, a human has to merge', which no capability that only reports a diff is allowed to say.
match: did i edit that generated file
local edits to a generated file

device-fix-evidence.label: prove a fix actually changed what the device shows, by measuring it
device-fix-evidence._why: Distinct from qa-testing (find the bug) and debugging (find the cause). This is the last step, and it is the one that silently does not happen, because on a real device the proof is a screenshot and every worthless screenshot looks like a good one from inside the transcript. A sleeping phone returns a black rectangle, a 401 from the debug bridge gets written to post.png as a JSON body, and a capture taken before the rebuild finished is a picture of the old binary. All three differ from the pre-fix capture, so a checksum comparison passes them and an eyeball reports the bug gone. It needs its own token because the honest answer is often UNVERIFIED, which is neither 'fixed' nor 'still broken', and no other capability here is allowed to return it.

device-toolchain-preflight.label: say whether a device build loop can run on this machine at all, before it starts
device-toolchain-preflight._why: Separate from every capability that DOES the work, because the answer is sometimes no and that has to be establishable in one command instead of discovered as a shell error three phases in. A skill that hands the model an xcodebuild line on Windows is not wrong about iOS, it is wrong about the machine, and the failure arrives after the agent has already edited source. It also needs its own token because 'no' here is not a failure state: a loop with a device half and an evidence half can still run the half that is pure file work, and saying which half is available is the actual deliverable.

ios-device-qa.label: exercise an iOS app on a real iPhone and report what it did
ios-device-qa._why: Separate from qa-testing, which assumes a URL and a browser, and from ios-development, which is writing and building the app. The distinguishing fact is the hardware: this work cannot begin without a paired phone, a Mac, and code compiled into the app under test, so 'yes' and 'not on this machine' are both complete answers and only this token can return the second one. Folding it into qa-testing is how a request to test an iPhone app gets answered with a headless browser pointed at nothing.
match: test the ios app on device
tap through the app on my phone
drive the app on the phone

remote-agent-authorization.label: decide what a remote agent or machine identity is allowed to do here, right now
remote-agent-authorization._why: Distinct from security-audit, which reads a codebase for weaknesses. This is a live decision with a yes or no, made per request against a grant file someone edited by hand, and its failure mode is unique: the answer that is wrong is indistinguishable from the answer that is right, because both are the word 'allowed'. The specific trap it exists to catch is a check that breaks and allows anyway, such as an expiry date the parser cannot read being treated as no expiry at all. It needs its own token because the correct response to an unreadable grant file is to deny everyone, and no capability whose job is to keep work moving is willing to say that.

ios-design-audit.label: audit the visual design of a native iOS app against the HIG
ios-design-audit._why: Distinct from design-review, which audits a live web page by querying a DOM for computed styles. There is no DOM here, so the mechanism is different in kind: half the rubric is decided by reading SwiftUI source (a fixed .system(size:) that ignores Dynamic Type, padding off the 4pt grid, a 28pt tap target, an icon-only Button with no VoiceOver label) and the other half needs a rendered screen on hardware that may not exist on this machine. Also distinct from ios-device-qa, which drives the app and reports what it did: this one is read-only and the deliverable is a score per dimension. It needs its own token because routing an iPhone design request to the browser skill produces an audit of nothing, and because the honest answer here is often partial in a way a web audit never is.

device-evidence-gate.label: refuse to score what no device was ever seen for
device-evidence-gate._why: The failure it catches is invisible by construction. A ten-dimension iOS rubric is ten questions a model can answer plausibly from source it just read, so a run on a machine with no Xcode, no simulator and no phone produces the same shaped report, with the same 0-10 scores and the same 'on real hardware' header, as a run on an actual iPhone. The blank screenshot is the same failure one level down: a backgrounded app captures as a structurally perfect PNG of solid black, gstack's own failure table names that case, and then hands the detection to the model that is looking at the same image. Separate from visual-evidence-ledger, which asks whether the screenshot opens; this asks whether anything was ever seen at all, and its correct answer is a dimension left UNSCORED rather than a number.
match: did you actually see the app
did it actually run on the phone
how do you know it looks
did you look at the app

debug-instrumentation-removal.label: take debug-only instrumentation back out of an app and prove none of it survives into a release build
debug-instrumentation-removal._why: The inverse of ios-debug-bridge-sync, which keeps instrumentation current, and not a case of code-review, which reads a diff someone wrote on purpose. Here the deliverable is an absence, and an absence is the one result you cannot see by looking at what is there. It needs its own token because the check everyone reaches for fails in both directions at once: a recursive grep for the package name exits non-zero on a path that does not exist, which inverts into a pass, and it also matches the comment somebody left saying the thing was removed, which makes a genuinely clean app permanently unable to satisfy it. Asked at exactly the moment nobody can afford a wrong answer, which is the week before a security audit or a store submission.
match: get gstack out of my app
before we submit to the app store
did i leave debug code in
is there debug code in the release build
is the debug server still in there
does the release build still open a port
make sure none of it ships

conditional-compilation-integrity.label: prove the #if / #endif blocks still balance after code was cut out of them
conditional-compilation-integrity._why: Separate from debugging, which starts from an error someone already saw. This starts from an edit that produced no error at all on the machine that made it. Deleting a debug-only block is the single most common way to leave a dangling #if, and the damage is uniquely invisible: the removed text is gone, so every search for it comes back empty and reports clean, while the file no longer compiles. On Windows there is no Swift compiler to say otherwise, so 'it built fine' is not available either and the defect travels to CI. It needs its own token because the subject is the directive structure itself, not the code inside it, and no capability that reads code for meaning ever counts the braces.
match: did i break the #if debug block
does it still compile after that
builds in debug but not release
release build fails after i removed

browser-cookie-import.label: move a logged-in session out of the real browser and into the headless one
browser-cookie-import._why: Distinct from browser-automation (drive a browser) and qa-testing (walk the app), because this is the step BEFORE either of those is worth doing. Almost everything worth checking on a product sits behind a login, and an anonymous headless session tests the marketing site instead. It needs its own token because the request arrives in the imperative ('use my session', 'log the browser in') and routing it to a general browser skill answers by opening a page that is not signed in.
match: test as a logged in user

session-auth-verification.label: prove the headless session is really signed in before anything is tested through it
session-auth-verification._why: Separate from browser-cookie-import (do the import) because the failure it catches reads as success on both sides of the wire. gstack's importer answers a domain it matched zero rows for with 'Imported 0 cookies for <domain>' and exit 0, and the page it then loads is a real page that renders fine, just logged out. So 'am I actually logged in' has to be answered from an artifact and a count, not from a screenshot that looks plausible. Route here whenever a check keeps landing on a sign-in screen, or when an authenticated result needs to be trusted.
match: it keeps showing the login page

cookie-encryption-diagnosis.label: explain why a browser's cookies cannot be read, by scheme and by count
cookie-encryption-diagnosis._why: 'There are no cookies' and 'you cannot decrypt these cookies' are opposite answers that produce the same empty list. Chrome 127+ on Windows uses App-Bound Encryption, whose key sits behind a SYSTEM-level DPAPI layer no unelevated same-user process can unwrap, so the correct output is a census and a refusal, not a retry. It needs its own token because every other capability here would answer by running the import again and getting the same empty result with more confidence.
match: which browser can i import from

markdown-document-export.label: turn a file you wrote into a document you can hand to a person
markdown-document-export._why: Separate from pdf-generation, which matches on the word 'pdf'. The request that actually arrives almost never says 'pdf': it says 'send this to the client', 'make me a one-pager', 'print this out'. The output format is an implementation detail of the errand, and a router that waits for the word 'pdf' misses the errand entirely.

pdf-output-verification.label: prove a PDF is a real document rather than a file with the right extension
pdf-output-verification._why: Producing a PDF and producing a DOCUMENT are different claims, and only the first one is what a renderer's exit code reports. A blank page, a page whose fonts are not embedded, and a page whose text layer copies out as 'S a i l i n g' all exit 0 everywhere. This token exists so 'is this thing actually okay' routes to a check on the artifact instead of to another render.

stack-self-upgrade.label: move this stack to a newer release of itself
stack-self-upgrade._why: A stack that ships over npx has to be able to replace its own installed files, which is the one operation where the tool doing the work is the thing being overwritten. It needs its own token because the request arrives as maintenance ('update yourself') rather than as work on the user's project, and every other capability here would answer it by editing the repository in front of it.

upgrade-verification.label: prove an upgrade actually landed on disk instead of trusting the installer's exit code
upgrade-verification._why: Separate from stack-self-upgrade because 'install the new version' and 'is the new version really what is on disk' are answered by different evidence, and only the second one survives a partial copy. gstack's upgrade prints 'gstack v{new} — upgraded from v{old}!' with {new} substituted from the version read BEFORE the upgrade ran, so a half-finished install and a clean one produce the same sentence. On Windows, where skills are file-copied rather than symlinked, one locked file is all it takes. Route here whenever someone doubts an install, not to another install.
match: the skill is still the old one

update-check-integrity.label: tell 'you are up to date' apart from 'the check for updates failed'
update-check-integrity._why: These are opposite answers that upstream prints identically. gstack's update check answers an unreachable registry by writing UP_TO_DATE into its cache and exiting 0, so a failed probe becomes a clean bill of health for the next hour; its cache expiry is decided by `find -mmin`, which Windows' find.exe does not implement, so on the wrong PATH order the cache never expires at all. This token exists so 'why does it keep saying I am current' routes to an audit of the check itself rather than to running the same check again and believing it.
match: it says im up to date
it says i'm up to date
why does it say up to date
it stopped telling me about updates

review-claim-lint.label: check a review's own file:line citations and counts against the tree it reviewed
review-claim-lint._why: Distinct from code-review (read the change) and from review-evidence-gate (did the review produce its artifacts). Here the artifacts exist and the question is whether what they say is true. A citation is the most persuasive sentence a review produces and the cheapest one to invent, because nothing downstream opens the file: line 214 of a 140-line spec reads exactly like line 214 of a 400-line one. It needs its own token because the answer is arithmetic against the working tree, and every capability that would otherwise take the request answers it by re-reading the review.
match: did you actually open that file

test-coverage-gap-audit.label: map every branch a change introduces and name the ones no test touches
test-coverage-gap-audit._why: Separate from qa-testing, which exercises a running app, and from generated-test-quality-gate, which asks whether one test asserts anything. This is the enumeration: every conditional, error path, early return and user journey in the planned change, each matched against a test that exists or marked as a gap. It needs its own token because the deliverable is a diagram rather than a verdict, and because a prose paragraph describing the branches satisfies every self-check while covering nothing.
match: before i implement, what needs tests

parallel-work-planning.label: split planned work into lanes that can run in separate worktrees without colliding
parallel-work-planning._why: Not planning-review (is this plan any good) and not shipping-deploy (land it). The subject is execution order across agents or worktrees, and the failure it prevents is specific and mechanical: two lanes declared independent while both edit the same module directory, which surfaces as a merge conflict hours later, after both lanes finished. It needs its own token because whether two lanes actually are independent is computable from the modules they name, and a capability that answers with a plan-shaped opinion will not compute it.
match: run these at the same time
can these two be done at once

post-ship-documentation.label: bring the docs back in line with what actually shipped, driven by the release diff
post-ship-documentation._why: Distinct from documentation, which is 'write or update a doc' as a standalone job. The defining input here is a diff that already landed: the work is not 'what should the README say' but 'what does the README now say that stopped being true when this branch merged'. It needs its own token because the request arrives immediately after shipping, in words that never mention docs at all ('did I forget anything', 'anything else before this merges'), and a router waiting for the word 'readme' misses it.
match: what does this need before merge

doc-claim-verification.label: prove a documentation file was really edited, rather than reported as edited
doc-claim-verification._why: Separate from documentation and from code-review because the subject is the REPORT, not the docs. The failure it catches is invisible from inside the conversation: the model that decided to edit README.md is the model that reports README.md as edited, from the same context window, with no read-back in between, so a run where the edit was planned and never applied prints exactly the table a successful run prints. Routing that here reaches the check that re-hashes the file and refuses the claim, instead of one that will summarise the intention again.
match: did it actually update the docs
i do not see the change

changelog-preservation.label: make sure polishing a changelog did not quietly rewrite the history under it
changelog-preservation._why: Its own token because the damage is silent and permanent, and because gstack's own skill records the incident that motivates it: an agent asked to polish the newest entry replaced the entries beneath it. A changelog is the one file in a repository whose older lines are supposed to be immutable, so 'reword the top entry' and 'regenerate the changelog' are one keystroke apart and only one of them is ever wanted. No capability whose job is to improve the writing is willing to refuse an improvement.

interaction-state-coverage.label: say what the screen shows while it loads, when it is empty, and when it fails
interaction-state-coverage._why: Separate from design-review, which audits a screen that already exists, and from planning-review, which asks whether a plan is any good overall. This is the narrow question asked BEFORE the code: are the four states nobody demos actually specified. It needs its own token because the failure it catches is invisible in a plan that reads as finished. A state table can be present, correctly shaped, and hold [spec] in every cell, which satisfies every self-check while specifying nothing. Whatever is left blank is what an engineer invents, which is how 'No items found.' ships as the empty state.
match: what does it show while loading
what happens when there are no results
what does the user see first
did we spec the empty state

ai-slop-detection.label: tell whether a design brief specifies decisions or recites the generated-website defaults
ai-slop-detection._why: Distinct from design-review (audit the pixels of a page that exists) and design-system (decide the rules once). The subject here is TEXT — a plan, a brief, a spec — and the question is whether it commits to anything. It needs its own token because the model asked to spot the pattern is usually the model that wrote it, so the request has to reach a skill that matches the written-down blacklist against the file with line numbers rather than one that will read the brief back and agree with itself.

mockup-reference-integrity.label: prove the mockup a plan tells someone to build from can still be opened
mockup-reference-integrity._why: Separate from design-exploration, which produces and compares variants in the moment, and from visual-evidence-ledger, which asks whether a screenshot backing a claim opens. This is about a path written into a document that outlives the conversation: an approved-mockup table is read weeks later, on another branch, by whoever implements. It needs its own token because the reference rots silently. A row citing a temp directory, an unexpanded $SLUG, or an API error body saved with a .png extension all read as a complete handoff in any review that only checks the table is present.
match: which mockup do i build from

developer-onboarding-review.label: review a plan for the people who will install, call, or read the thing being built
developer-onboarding-review._why: Distinct from planning-review, which asks whether a plan is any good, and from design-review, which audits what an end user sees. The subject here is the second audience: whoever integrates against this. It needs its own token because the rubric is different in kind — time to first working call, whether the interface is guessable without docs, what the error says at 2am — and because the first question it has to answer is what developer-facing surface even exists, which is read off the repository rather than inferred from the plan's prose. A plan that mentions a terminal is not a CLI.
match: would a developer figure this out
who is going to install this

getting-started-path-verification.label: prove the documented getting-started path actually runs in the repository it documents
getting-started-path-verification._why: Separate from documentation, which is about whether docs exist, and from qa-testing, which needs a running app. The failure it catches is invisible from inside the README, because the README reads perfectly: an `npm run dev` with no `dev` script in package.json, a `cp .env.example .env` with no .env.example in the repo, a copy-paste block still holding YOUR_API_KEY. Every one of those is a dead end on the first thing a new developer does, and none of them can be found by reading the file that contains them — only by resolving its commands against the repository. It needs its own token because 'time to hello world' is otherwise always an estimate, and an estimate is the wrong answer when a step does not run at all.
match: the setup steps do not work
can a new dev run this

error-message-quality.label: measure whether error messages tell a developer what happened and what to do next
error-message-quality._why: Separate from debugging, which starts from an error someone is trying to fix, and from code-review, which reads a diff. Here the error messages ARE the product surface, and the question is whether each one names the value that caused it, says what to do, and links anywhere. It needs its own token because the alternative is a model picking three errors to talk about, which selects for the ones it can talk about rather than the ones that are worst. A census scores all of them and lets the count choose which three get traced.
match: what will they see when it breaks

dx-review-continuity.label: know whether this project's developer experience has been reviewed before, and refuse to call a lookup that failed an absence
dx-review-continuity._why: Separate from relationship-continuity, which is history about the person, and from retrospective, which looks back at shipped work. This is history about one dimension of one project, and it exists because the trend columns of a DX scorecard are worthless when they are filled from memory. The failure it catches reads as a clean first review: gstack keys its review log by branch, so a project on its fourth DX review is told it is on its first, and every other way that lookup can break — a missing reader, an unreadable directory, a slug that resolved differently this run — lands on the same NO_PRIOR_DX_REVIEWS string. Route here when someone asks whether the DX got better, because the honest answer is sometimes 'the history could not be read', which is not the same as none.
match: what did the last review say

check-runner-integrity.label: tell 'the checks passed' apart from 'the checks did not run'
check-runner-integrity._why: Separate from code-health, which asks how good the code is. This asks whether the thing that measured it measured anything, and the two answers look identical on a dashboard. gstack's /health reads a tool's exit code as `tool | tail -50; EXIT_CODE=$?`, which is tail's status and is therefore 0 forever, so a type checker exiting 2 is recorded as clean and scored 10/10; its detector is zsh and finds no checks at all on a Windows Python or PowerShell project, and its own rule says a skipped tool must not penalise the score. Everything green and nothing measured is the single most expensive false positive a quality tool can produce, and it needs its own token because every capability that answers 'is the code okay' will answer this by running the same broken check again.
match: it passed but it is broken

quality-trend.label: say whether code quality moved, and refuse to call a changed measurement a change in quality
quality-trend._why: Distinct from code-health (score it now) and from retrospective (what did we ship). The subject is two runs and the gap between them, and the failure it exists to catch is arithmetic: when a tool's weight is redistributed on the runs where it is missing, DELETING the check that was dragging the average raises the composite exactly like fixing the code would, and gstack's history line records only the scores, so 'Trend: IMPROVING (+0.9)' is what both look like. Route here when someone asks whether things got better, because the honest answer is sometimes that the two numbers are not comparable.
match: better or worse than last week
compare to the last health check

diagram-artifact-verification.label: prove a rendered diagram is a diagram, not a file with the right extension
diagram-artifact-verification._why: Separate from diagramming, which asks for a picture to be drawn. This asks whether the picture that already exists says anything, and its failures are silent by construction. A renderer whose promise never resolved writes the literal string "undefined" into the .svg; a mermaid error graphic is a structurally valid SVG; a screenshot taken before the page painted is a perfect PNG of one flat colour; a scene file with an empty elements array opens as a blank canvas. All four exit 0 everywhere, and all four read as a delivery in a transcript. Routing here reaches the check that reads the file back off disk and refuses it, rather than a skill that will render it again.
match: labels are missing from the diagram

editable-diagram-handoff.label: hand over a diagram the other person can open and change
editable-diagram-handoff._why: Distinct from diagramming because the deliverable is not the image, it is the editability. 'Draw me a box' is satisfied by a raster; 'so I can move that box' needs a scene file plus a source that can be re-rendered, and a raster answers it wrongly while looking correct. It needs its own token because the honest answer is sometimes no: only flowcharts convert to an editable scene, so a sequence diagram handed over as editable is a promise that breaks in front of whoever opens it.
match: put a diagram in the readme

design-implementation.label: turn a chosen design into production markup in the framework this repo actually uses
design-implementation._why: Distinct from design-exploration (pick a direction), design-system (decide the rules) and design-review (audit a screen that exists). Here the decision is already made and the deliverable is code that lands in the repo. It needs its own token because the request is silently two requests — what to build AND what to build it in — and a router that only hears the first sends it somewhere that answers with a standalone HTML file. gstack's version greps package.json for "react" and takes the first match, so every Next.js repo is classified React and Tailwind is never seen at all; the file that comes back has no client boundary and its own palette. Whether the output is a server component, a client component, or one .html is not a preference, it is a fact about the repo, and it has to be read off disk before a line is written.
design-implementation._matchNote: "mockup into" is here rather than the fuller "turn the mockup into code" because the matcher is substring-based, and the sentence a person actually types is "turn this mockup into a component", which contains neither of the longer phrases. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

markup-quality-gate.label: check generated markup against accessibility, token and slop rules before anyone calls it done
markup-quality-gate._why: Separate from design-review, which is a human eye on a rendered screen, and from code-review, which reads a diff for defects. The subject is markup that a model just wrote, and the reviewer is the same model, which is why the answer has to come from something that exits non-zero rather than from a reading. gstack carries the identical rules — the AI slop blacklist, the alt attributes, the reduced-motion guard, never lorem ipsum — as bullet points in a markdown file addressed to the model about to break them, so nothing executes and 'done' is self-asserted. It needs its own token because the honest verdict includes a third state nobody asks for: the file was empty, unreadable, or of a type with no rules behind it, and reporting that as a pass is worse than reporting a finding.
match: did i use the design tokens

client-boundary-audit.label: find components using client-only React in a server component, before the build does
client-boundary-audit._why: Routing this to debugging gets an investigation of a symptom that a whole-tree scan answers in one pass, because the defect is structural rather than a bug in any one line: in the Next App Router every file is a server component until a directive says otherwise, so useState in a file with no "use client" is not wrong code, it is code in the wrong place. It earns a token because the feedback arrives at build or first render rather than at write time, which means it is reliably introduced by exactly the workflow that generates several components at once and never runs them.
match: only works in a client component
why does this need use client

local-preview-server.label: serve generated markup locally and prove something is actually answering on the URL
local-preview-server._why: Not browser-automation, which drives a browser that already has somewhere to go. This is the step before: putting the file at an address. It needs its own token because the failure is a lie rather than an error. gstack starts the server with `python3 -m http.server 0` and then recovers the kernel-assigned port with lsof, so on Windows, where lsof does not exist and python3 is the Microsoft Store alias stub, the variable is empty and the skill announces 'Live preview running at http://localhost:/finalized.html' with nothing running and its documented `open` fallback also missing. A preview that reports success it did not verify wastes the one thing the preview existed to buy, which is the user looking at it.
match: show me what it looks like

question-suppression.label: stop the agent asking a question it has already been answered, without stopping the ones that cannot be undone
question-suppression._why: Not user-memory, which stores what the person is like and is read by a model that may or may not act on it. This is the enforcement half: a policy file plus a PreToolUse hook that removes the prompt before it is rendered, so it works when the model forgets. It needs its own token because the request arrives as an interruption rather than a task ('stop asking me that') and the only useful answer changes a hook's behaviour, not the current turn's. gstack has the idea and calls its version observational; on Windows its enforcement hook builds the path to its own door-type registry with new URL(import.meta.url).pathname, so the file is never found, all twelve one-way doors default to two-way, and a never-ask preference auto-approves a production rollback.

question-policy-inspection.label: show which questions are being suppressed, prove the suppression is real, and undo it
question-policy-inspection._why: Split from question-suppression because setting a policy and auditing one have opposite risk profiles. Setting is cheap and reversible; auditing is what you do when you suspect something was decided for you, and the honest output includes the cases where the policy is stored but inert. Kept as its own token so 'what did you decide without me' cannot be routed to the thing that decides more without you.
match: what did you decide for me

cross-session-learning.label: keep, recall and prune what has been learned about this project across sessions
cross-session-learning._why: Distinct from user-memory, which is what the person told the agent about how THEY work, and from context-read, which resumes one session's work in progress. The subject here is durable knowledge about the codebase, and the store outlives every session that wrote to it. It needs its own token mainly because of the question that makes such a store worth having at all: not 'is there a learning about this' but 'how many times has this already cost me', which is arithmetic over recurrences rather than a recollection. gstack's store cannot answer it — its preamble counts the file with wc -l, which counts rows rather than sightings and silently drops the last one whenever the file does not end in a newline.
match: what do we know about this project
why do i keep making this mistake

learning-store-integrity.label: tell 'nothing has been learned' apart from 'the learnings could not be read'
learning-store-integrity._why: Two opposite answers that upstream prints identically, and the wrong one is the one that ends the search. gstack's reader pipes the store through `bun -e` and ends with `2>/dev/null || exit 0`, so with bun absent — it is not a Claude Code dependency — a store holding three rows prints nothing and exits 0, and the `|| echo "No learnings yet."` fallback written into gstack's own SKILL.md never fires either, because exiting 0 is not a failure. One corrupt line does the same thing in miniature: four rows on disk, `LEARNINGS: 1 loaded`, no warning, exit 0. Nothing can be written back from PowerShell to repair it either, because PowerShell 5.1 strips embedded double quotes when it builds a native process's command line, so `gstack-learnings-log '<json>'` answers every call with 'invalid JSON, skipping' and exit 1. This token exists so a doubted store routes to a reader that fails closed with a line number, rather than to another read that will confidently report zero.

shipped-work-audit.label: count what actually landed in a window, out of git, rather than out of memory
shipped-work-audit._why: A narrower token than retrospective, which is the whole ritual: praise, habits, trend tables, tone. This is the arithmetic underneath it, and the two requests fail differently. 'How was the week' tolerates an impression; 'did that actually ship' is asked precisely when someone suspects their memory and the repository disagree, and an impression is the one answer that is useless there. The failure it catches is a confident narrative built on nothing: gstack's retro guards the window with `git remote | grep -c '^origin$' || echo 0`, and because grep -c PRINTS 0 and EXITS 1 the variable holds two lines and never equals "0", so the branch that exists to say 'do not trust this window' is unreachable; the run then does `git log origin/<default> | grep -v '^$' | sort | uniq -c`, where a nonexistent ref puts fatal: on stderr while the pipeline still exits 0, so a broken query and a quiet week hand the model the identical empty result. Route here when someone asks what really landed, because the honest answer is sometimes that the window was empty or the ref was wrong, and neither of those is a smaller week.

cross-repo-activity.label: measure work across every project at once, not just the repo you happen to be standing in
cross-repo-activity._why: Separate from shipped-work-audit because the unit of the answer is the portfolio rather than the repository, and because the question is usually about attention, not output: which project ate the week, and which one has quietly not been touched in a month. It earns its own token because its failure mode is the opposite of a single-repo retro's. There the risk is a fabricated week; here it is a silently SHORT list, where the repos that could not be read simply do not appear and the totals still look complete. gstack reaches this through a bun-compiled discovery binary that indexes AI-tool session files and writes diagnostics to /tmp, neither of which exists on a Windows box that installed gstack rather than building it, and it reports the losses as the prose footnote 'N repos could not be reached'. Route here when someone asks about all their projects, because a per-project table with a named failure row is the only version of that answer anyone can check.
match: which project did i work on
what have i been working on

live-dx-audit.label: walk the product's own getting-started flow for real and report what happened
live-dx-audit._why: Distinct from developer-onboarding-review, which reviews a PLAN before anything exists, and from getting-started-path-verification, which resolves the README's commands against the repository statically without running them or opening a browser. Here the product is already up and the request is to be the new developer: open the page, run the install, hit the error. It needs its own token because the failure it catches is the reassuring kind. gstack's live audit spends `$B`, a shell variable set in one Bash call and empty in every call after it, so `$B goto <url>` becomes bash's own `goto` and exits 127 with empty stdout; the skill has no state anywhere for 'the screenshot did not happen', and its scorecard's evidence column is the literal token [screenshots]. A run in which nothing was ever loaded produces the same document as a run in which everything was.
match: install it like a new user
pretend you are a new developer

onboarding-timing-evidence.label: put a real clock on how long getting started takes, instead of estimating it
onboarding-timing-evidence._why: Separate from live-dx-audit because it is the one number the whole audit is judged on and the one most likely to be invented. gstack's scorecard row reads `TTHW (measured)` and the per-step cells it is summed from read `Time: [est]` in the same file: it says estimate on one line and measured on another about the same number. Route here when someone doubts a duration, because the honest answer comes from a monotonic clock and a step list anyone can re-sum, not from a model's sense of how long a page took.
match: how long does it take to get started
how long to first working call
is that number measured or guessed
where does that number come from

dx-audit-artifact.label: leave a developer-experience audit on disk, with the screenshots and logs its scores were computed from
dx-audit-artifact._why: Separate from visual-evidence-ledger, which asks whether one screenshot opens, and from review-evidence-gate, which asks whether a review pipeline produced its per-phase outputs. The subject here is a DX scorecard specifically, and the failure is that it is a template: eight rows of blank score cells with [screenshots] and [file refs] for evidence, which pasted unfilled is a finished-looking audit nobody can check and nothing can diff against next month. Route here when someone asks where the audit went, what backs a score, or wants this run compared with the last one, because the answer has to be a directory rather than a paragraph.
match: show me the evidence for that score
did the audit actually load anything
compare this dx run to the last one
re-run the dx audit after the fixes

adversarial-second-opinion.label: have a different model, from a different vendor, attack the change
adversarial-second-opinion._why: Distinct from code-review, which is this model reading its own diff. The defining property is independence: the whole value comes from the reviewer not being the author, so the request cannot be satisfied by reviewing harder. It needs its own token because the honest answer is sometimes that no second opinion is available on this machine, and every capability whose job is to review will answer it by reviewing.

external-reviewer-preflight.label: establish whether the outside reviewer can actually run and authenticate here, before anything is planned around it
external-reviewer-preflight._why: Separate from the review itself, because the answer is sometimes no and a no has to arrive before an expensive prompt is built rather than as unparsed stderr afterwards. The failure it catches is specific: a name on PATH is not a working program, and a credential file that exists is not a credential. gstack tests the first with `command -v codex` and the second with `[ -f auth.json ]`, so a 0-byte auth.json answers AUTH_OK (reproduced on Windows, 2026-08-14) and the skill proceeds toward a review it will never get.
external-reviewer-preflight._matchNote: The matcher is substring-based, so the phrase a person actually types has to be in here. "codex return nothing" is present alongside "codex returned nothing" because "why did codex return nothing" contains neither the past tense nor "do nothing". Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

review-gate-integrity.label: tell 'the reviewer found nothing' apart from 'the reviewer never spoke'
review-gate-integrity._why: Two opposite results that a marker-absence gate spells identically. gstack's rule is 'if no [P1] markers are found, the gate is PASS', and on Windows its Codex output reaches that rule as zero bytes: the JSONL is piped through python3, which is the Microsoft Store alias stub, so `command -v python3` succeeds, gstack's own 'Python 3 is required' guard never fires, and PIPESTATUS[0] reports codex's exit status rather than the parser's. A [P1] SQL-injection finding was reproduced becoming GATE: PASS this way. It needs its own token because the correct verdict is a third one, UNVERIFIED, which no capability obliged to return pass or fail is able to give.

documentation-authoring.label: write documentation that does not exist yet, partitioned by which reader need it serves
documentation-authoring._why: Split from documentation, which is 'edit the docs', and from post-ship-documentation, which is driven by a diff that already landed. The defining input here is absence: there is no document, and the first real decision is which of the four Diataxis quadrants the missing thing belongs to, because a tutorial and a reference for the same feature are different documents with different readers and mixing them produces something neither reader can use. It needs its own token because the request never names a file ('nobody else can run this', 'how would someone else use it'), so a router waiting for the word readme sends it to the skill that edits an existing one.
match: how would someone else use this

citation-verification.label: check that a document's file paths, symbols, flags, links and line citations point at things that actually exist
citation-verification._why: Separate from doc-claim-verification, which asks whether a file was really edited. This asks whether what the file SAYS is real. Documentation is the one artifact a language model is graded on plausibility by a reader who cannot check it, and the failure is silent: a fabricated `makeWidget()` next to a real `createWidget()` reads exactly like correct prose until somebody copies it. gstack's countermeasure is a self-review checkbox, 'Every API description matches the actual code signature', ticked by the same context window that wrote the description with no read-back in between. Routing here reaches the check that resolves every name against the source and prints the closest real one.
match: is that actually in the code
check the docs against the code

api-surface-extraction.label: list what the code really declares, each with the file and line it was read from
api-surface-extraction._why: The input any honest reference document needs, and the thing no model can supply from recall. Distinct from code-review, which judges a change, and from post-ship-documentation, which reads a diff: this reads the tree and answers 'what could somebody type', which is the question a reference doc is an answer to. It is a separate token because it is also the useful answer to a question that is not about docs at all ('what does this export'), and because on Windows gstack's version of this step is a `find . -type f | head -200` that returns 'FIND: Parameter format not correct' and nothing else.
match: what env vars does this read
what files are in this project

doc-discoverability.label: measure how many clicks a document really is from the entry point, over the actual link graph
doc-discoverability._why: A document nothing links to is a document nobody reads, which makes it indistinguishable from a document nobody wrote. gstack states the rule ('every new document must be reachable within 2 clicks from README.md') inside the step where the agent is asked to confirm it about the files it just created, so the rule is only ever as good as the recollection of the thing being audited. Its own token because the request is usually about the outcome rather than the graph ('would a new person find this'), and because the honest answer is a number.
match: would a new person find this
is it linked from the readme
how do people find this doc
is it in the table of contents

video-production.label: turn a plain sentence into a finished, rendered video
video-production._why: Every other token here describes work on a repository; this one produces a file that is not code, and the request arrives in a register nothing else matches. 'make me a video showing off X' has no verb any of the tokens above recognise, so before this existed it routed to nothing at all, or to design-review on the word 'looks'. It also has a cost profile of its own: a wrong guess about aspect ratio throws away minutes of encoding rather than seconds of reading, which is why the skill behind it is allowed to ask a question and the rest are not.
video-production._matchNote: Deliberately NOT here: 'record the screen', 'take a screenshot', 'gif'. Those are capture requests that browse and qa already own, and a capture is not an edit. Also not here: bare 'edit' or 'render', which collide with editing code and rendering a page. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

visible-browser-session.label: open a browser window a person can watch, and prove it is really open
visible-browser-session._why: Separate from browser-automation because the two answer opposite questions. browser-automation asks 'can something drive a page', and the fastest yes is headless. This asks 'can a HUMAN see it happen', and headless is a flat no. The requests that need it are the ones where the evidence is the watching: a login the person has to complete by hand, a cookie wall a fresh headless profile cannot pass, a flow someone wants to see with their own eyes before believing it. Folding it into browser-automation routes every one of those to the headless daemon, which does the work perfectly and shows nobody anything.
visible-browser-session._matchNote: "take a screenshot" and "verify the page" are deliberately NOT here. A screenshot is evidence produced FOR a person, not a window shown TO one, and browse already owns it and is faster. Putting them here would pull ordinary QA onto a browser launch that costs seven seconds and a visible window. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

browser-extension-integrity.label: check the browser sidebar extension is really installed and loadable before anything relies on it
browser-extension-integrity._why: The sidebar is the whole reason to open a visible browser, and it is the part most likely to be quietly absent: it lives in a directory whose name depends on which agent tool installed gstack, and a missing one produces a browser window that looks completely normal. It gets its own token so 'the side panel is empty' and 'the extension will not load' route to the thing that reads the manifest off disk, rather than to a browser launch that will cheerfully succeed and prove nothing.

browser-session-teardown.label: stop a running browser session without leaving it orphaned
browser-session-teardown._why: Closing is not the reverse of opening and cannot share its token. Opening can be retried; a bad close leaves a process nothing on the machine has a record of, holding a port and a profile lock, and the next open then fails for a reason that points nowhere. It also has its own failure mode worth routing to on purpose: 'the browser is still running' and 'port 34567 is in use' are reports ABOUT a teardown that already went wrong.

browser-agent-pairing.label: hand another agent access to this machine's browser, on purpose and on the record
browser-agent-pairing._why: Separate from browser-automation, which asks whether something can drive a page. This asks who else may drive it, and the answer is a credential that leaves the machine. It is also separate from remote-agent-authorization, which reads an existing grant and answers yes or no: this token is the moment the grant is created, where the defaults decide everything and the person is the only one who can widen them. It exists because 'share my browser' arrives sounding like a convenience and is in fact the largest single-command privilege transfer in the stack.
browser-agent-pairing._matchNote: "open the browser" and "control my browser" are deliberately NOT here; they belong to visible-browser-session, which shows a window to the person sitting there rather than giving a credential to something that is not. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.
match: let another agent use my browser

grant-revocation-proof.label: take access back, and prove it actually went away
grant-revocation-proof._why: A revoke is the one operation whose failure looks exactly like its success: the command returns, nobody objects, and the other party still has the key. It needs its own token because the useful answer is never the word revoked, it is the re-read that shows the session gone, and no capability whose job is to perform an action is in the habit of checking afterwards. It also carries the questions that come later, 'who has access' and 'did that ever get cut off', which are audits rather than actions.
grant-revocation-proof._matchNote: Deliberately NOT here: "rotate the key" and "new api key", which are credential management for services this stack does not hold. Verified with route.mjs explain before and after.

_comment: These decide whether the marketplace tier is even eligible. They exist so that
'offer to search the marketplace' is a computed verdict with printed reasons, not a
mood. If the gate says no, the router says nothing about the marketplace at all.

antiSignals._comment: Any of these present and the marketplace tier is refused, whatever else matched.

completionPhrases._comment: Signals that a finished, reusable artifact now exists. Used for the sell tier.

gates._minSpecificTermsWhy: The Toolbay server's matcher strips stopwords and needs at least two distinct specific terms, so a vaguer query is guaranteed to return nothing. Refusing to send it is cheaper and more honest than sending it and reporting an empty result.
